title: Strike Season Starts on Your Load Board: Canadian Trucking's 2027 Port and Rail Labour Calendar
summary: Canada's rail and port contracts expire from late 2026 through 2027. Here is how carriers and brokers should plan capacity, accessorials and reroutes now.
body_markdown:
## The decision is due before the strike vote


Most Canadian freight teams treat a rail or port stoppage as an event. You watch the news, a strike notice drops, and the phones light up. The shops that came out of 2023 and 2024 with their margins and their customers intact treated it as a calendar instead. Right now that calendar is unusually crowded.


According to a September 10, 2026 national business-press analysis, the collective agreement between one of Canada's two Class I railways and its rail workers expires at the end of this year. The agreement covering West Coast dockworkers expires about three months after that. About nine months later, the other Class I railway hits its own contract deadline. That puts three national-scale bargaining rounds inside roughly 12 months, and two of them land in the first quarter of 2027, when intermodal-dependent shippers are already rebuilding inventory after peak.


The real question for an operator isn't whether a stoppage happens. It's which of your loads, lanes and contracts quietly assume that one won't, and what you've committed to customers if it does.


## What the last two rounds actually cost


We have recent evidence. In 2023, a strike shut the West Coast ports in Vancouver and Prince Rupert for 13 days and disrupted about $10 billion in cargo. On August 22, 2024, both Class I railways locked out about 9,300 engineers, conductors and yard workers at the same time, the first simultaneous national freight-rail stoppage in Canadian history. By day one, about 830,000 tonnes of goods worth roughly $1.1 billion had stopped moving.


Then in November 2024, container terminals across British Columbia were locked out from November 4, alongside disputes at the ports of Montréal and Québec. On November 12, 2024, the federal labour minister used section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board to order operations to resume and to impose final binding arbitration.


Two lessons from those rounds matter more to trucking than the headline numbers.


First, the damage starts before the stoppage and lasts after it. Railways wind down sensitive traffic ahead of a deadline, terminals stop accepting certain cargo, and embargo notices show up days before anyone walks out. After a restart, the backlog takes weeks to clear. Your drivers sit at congested ramps and terminals well after the news cycle has moved on.


Second, some freight never comes back. The federal Industrial Inquiry Commission that reviewed the 2023 port strike found that U.S. marine terminals signed long-term contracts with shippers during the shutdown, capturing business that had moved through Canada. For a Canadian drayage or transload operation, that isn't a two-week dip. It's a permanent change in lane mix.


## Bill C-39 changes the clock, not the risk


On September 21, 2026, Ottawa introduced Bill C-39, an omnibus economic bill with significant amendments to Part I of the Canada Labour Code. It hasn't passed, and the labour provisions come into force on proclamation, so how they apply to rounds already underway is something to watch rather than assume. As drafted, though, the bill rewrites the timing that freight planners rely on:


-


**Longer conciliation.** Mandatory conciliation goes from 60 days to 90 days. Parties still can't strike or lock out until at least 21 days after conciliation ends, so a lawful stoppage is pushed back by at least a month.


-


**A special mediator with a public report.** The minister can appoint a special mediator for 21 days before day 75 of conciliation. If there's no deal, that mediator's report on the issues and each side's positions is made public five days after the mandate ends.


-


**Mandatory early bargaining for contentious units.** Where the last agreement came from binding arbitration, followed a strike or lockout, or ran five years or more, bargaining has to start 200 to 180 days before expiry.


-


**A codified section 107.** The minister could end a stoppage, extend an agreement or order binding arbitration only after considering the special mediator's report and concluding the dispute affects or may affect the national interest.


For context, the same analysis notes that section 107 was rarely used for decades and then invoked nine times in two years. The bill keeps that tool in place and adds procedure around it. Unions have raised objections, with longshore workers arguing the changes would effectively remove their right to strike, and constitutional challenges to earlier section 107 use are ongoing.


For an ops leader, the practical read is simple. If C-39 passes in roughly its current form, you get a longer, more visible run-up to any stoppage and a published report that tells you how far apart the parties are. That's more warning, not less exposure. The shops that benefit are the ones that turn each public milestone (notice to bargain, conciliation request, special mediator appointment, report release) into a planned operational trigger instead of a reason to start a meeting.


## Where Canadian trucking actually breaks


A port or rail stoppage doesn't hit every carrier or broker the same way. Here's where it usually breaks.


**Drayage and ramp-dependent freight.** If your volume is container drayage out of Vancouver, Prince Rupert or Montréal, or ramp work at inland intermodal terminals, a stoppage takes away your origin. You may face a shortage of work and a pile of street-turn, storage and per diem disputes at the same time.


**Rail-dependent bulk and long-haul.** Grain, potash, lumber, chemicals and other freight that normally moves by rail can't simply be absorbed by trucks. A grain analyst quoted in that analysis compared moving grain by truck to emptying a bathtub with a spoon. The truck opportunity is real but narrow, and it's often priced on panic rather than on lanes you can actually sustain.


**Dangerous goods and temperature-controlled.** These are usually the first commodities the railways restrict ahead of a deadline. If you haul or broker them, your exposure starts earlier than the strike date.


**Cross-border reroutes.** When Canadian gateways close, some import freight lands at U.S. Pacific Northwest or U.S. East Coast ports and comes into Canada by highway. That brings in-bond moves through the U.S., bonded carrier requirements, ACI eManifest timing and CBSA release questions that a domestic-only fleet may not be set up for. A reroute that adds a border crossing is a compliance project, not just a longer lane.


## Asset, broker and hybrid tradeoffs


**Asset carriers** decide how much capacity to hold in reserve for surge truckload and transload work versus keeping it committed to contract lanes. Holding trucks idle against a strike that gets averted at the last minute is expensive. Committing everything to contract freight means your best customers watch you miss the spike. Many fleets settle on a defined surge pool with pre-agreed rates for named customers, triggered by specific milestones, instead of a loose promise to help.


**Brokers** have more flexibility on capacity and more exposure on commitments. The common failure is quoting rail-to-truck conversions on spot terms while carrying a contract rate with the shipper that assumed rail economics. If your shipper contracts don't spell out what happens when the intended mode is unavailable, you're the one absorbing the difference.


**Hybrid operators** often have the best position on paper and the messiest one in practice. Asset trucks, brokered capacity and sometimes a transload or warehouse footprint all compete for the same surge freight. Without clear rules about which freight goes to company trucks first, which goes to the broker desk, and how intercompany pricing works, the business ends up bidding against itself.


## What to set up before January


None of this needs a new system. It needs your existing workflows to recognize that some loads are exposed to a labour calendar.


1.


**Tag dependency at the load and lane level.** Mark which freight depends on a specific port, ramp or rail carrier, and which customers have alternative modes. If you can't pull a list today of every active lane that touches a Canadian Class I ramp or a West Coast container terminal, start there.


2.


**Map milestones to actions.** Notice to bargain, conciliation request, special mediator appointment, report release, strike notice and the embargo itself should each trigger a defined step, such as confirming surge rates, pre-positioning chassis, notifying named customers or pausing new commitments on exposed lanes.


3.


**Build the statuses you'll need.** An "embargo hold" or "terminal closed" status that stops the detention clock correctly, routes the exception to the right desk and tells the customer what's happening is worth more than a dozen emails during the event.


4.


**Pre-write the accessorial and reroute terms.** Storage, re-delivery, extended free time, reroute miles, border crossing and in-bond handling should be defined charges with approval rules, not things you argue about after the fact. Check your force majeure language with shippers and carriers before you need it.


5.


**Decide who gets capacity first.** Write down the allocation rules for surge freight by customer tier, contract status and margin. Then put those rules where dispatch and the broker desk actually work, so they aren't relitigated load by load.


6.


**Plan the cross-border version.** If you might take rerouted freight through U.S. ports, confirm bonded carrier status, eManifest workflows and customs broker handoffs now, while it's quiet.


Every freight business carries its exposure differently. A Prince George lumber hauler, a Montréal drayage fleet and a Toronto non-asset broker will each write a different version of this list. That's the point. The rules, statuses, permissions and billing logic in your operating system should reflect your exposure, not a generic template that assumes the rail is always running.


## The bottom line


Canada is heading into a stretch where rail and port bargaining rounds overlap, and the federal government is changing the process while those rounds are already on the calendar. Whether or not a stoppage happens, the run-up will move freight, rates and customer expectations. The operators who come out ahead will have decided in October and November what they'll do in February.


## FAQ


### When do Canada's major rail and port labour agreements expire?


One Class I railway's agreement with its rail workers expires at the end of 2026, the West Coast dockworker agreement expires about three months later, and the other Class I railway's agreement expires about nine months after that, according to a September 2026 national business-press analysis.


### What does Bill C-39 change for strikes at Canadian ports and railways?


As introduced on September 21, 2026, Bill C-39 would extend mandatory conciliation from 60 to 90 days, add a 21-day special mediator whose report is made public, require early bargaining for some units, and set conditions for the minister to use section 107. It hasn't been passed, and its labour provisions take effect on proclamation.


### Can trucks replace rail during a Canadian rail stoppage?


Only partly. Trucks can absorb some time-sensitive and higher-value freight, but bulk commodities like grain and potash move in volumes that highway capacity can't realistically replace, so carriers should price and commit to surge work carefully.


### How should brokers protect margin during a port or rail disruption?


Brokers should make sure shipper contracts define what happens when the intended mode is unavailable, pre-agree surge and reroute rates, and set clear accessorial terms for storage, re-delivery and border handling before a stoppage starts.


### What should Canadian carriers do if import freight is rerouted through U.S. ports?


Confirm bonded carrier status for in-bond moves, have ACI eManifest and CBSA release workflows ready, and coordinate customs broker handoffs in advance, because a reroute adds a border crossing and compliance steps to the lane.
